title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
author: Frederick Douglass
setting: Talbot County and Baltimore, Maryland, with the last chapter in New York and New Bedford, Massachusetts
lengthNote: Eleven short chapters and an appendix, preceded by a preface and a letter from two white abolitionists
openingLine: I was born in Tuckahoe, near Hillsborough, and about twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot County, Maryland.
summary: Douglass opens by saying what he does not know: his age, his birthday, his father. From that missing record he builds an argument, because the record is missing by design. The book follows a boy from a Maryland plantation to a Baltimore kitchen where a woman begins to teach him the alphabet, to a field where he fights the man hired to break him, and finally to a Massachusetts wharf where he is paid for his labour. It is testimony rather than fiction, and it was published while its author could still be seized and returned.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
sourceText.note: This is a memoir, so everyone listed under characters below is a real person. Douglass names his enslavers, overseers and employers, and gives the counties they lived in; several of them were alive and identifiable when the book appeared, which is part of what made publishing it dangerous.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: By the Anti-Slavery Office in Boston, seven years after Douglass escaped and four years after he first spoke publicly at Nantucket.

atAGlance.label: Full title
atAGlance.value: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave. Written by Himself.
atAGlance.note: The last three words are the argument of the title page: readers were expected to doubt that the author existed.

atAGlance.label: Before the text
atAGlance.note: William Lloyd Garrison and Wendell Phillips vouch for the book at length before its author is allowed to begin.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The appendix is not an afterthought: it separates the Christianity Douglass holds from the religion practised by the men in the preceding chapters.

structure.label: Preface and Letter
structure.title: Two white men introduce a black author
structure.summary: Garrison recalls hearing Douglass speak at Nantucket and insists the book is entirely his own work. Phillips writes about the danger of printing names and places while the law can still take a man back. Both documents assume a reader who needs persuading that the author is real.

scenes.title: Garrison's testimonial
scenes.summary: An account of the 1841 Nantucket convention, and a guarantee that nothing in the book has been softened.

scenes.title: Phillips on the risk
scenes.summary: Publishing under his own name, in a country with a fugitive slave law, exposes Douglass to recapture.

structure.label: Chapters I–IV
structure.title: Tuckahoe, and the great house farm
structure.summary: Douglass records a birth without a date, a mother he saw perhaps five times, and the whipping of his aunt in a kitchen doorway. He then widens the lens: the allowance of food and clothing, the songs on the road to the great house farm, and three overseers whose killings produced no inquest.

scenes.title: What is not known
scenes.summary: No record of his age, no acknowledged father, and the law that makes a child follow its mother's condition.

scenes.title: The songs
scenes.summary: Colonel Lloyd's plantation as an economy, and the singing that northern readers have misheard as contentment.

scenes.title: Overseers
scenes.summary: Gore, Severe and the killing of Demby: three deaths, and no prosecution in any of them.

structure.label: Chapters V–VII
structure.title: A city, a kitchen and an alphabet
structure.summary: Sent to Hugh Auld's house in Baltimore, Douglass is taught his letters by Sophia Auld until her husband stops the lessons and explains, in front of the pupil, exactly why reading is dangerous. Douglass takes the explanation as a syllabus and continues on the street, in a shipyard and out of a borrowed schoolbook.

scenes.title: The passage to Baltimore
scenes.summary: A sloop down the Miles River, and a household where he is fed enough to notice the difference.

scenes.title: The prohibition
scenes.summary: Hugh Auld forbids the lessons and supplies the reason; Sophia Auld begins to change.

scenes.title: The Columbian Orator
scenes.summary: Bread traded for lessons, a schoolbook of speeches, and the discovery that reading brings no relief with it.

structure.label: Chapters VIII–IX
structure.title: Valued with the livestock
structure.summary: Captain Anthony's death sends Douglass back to be appraised alongside the horses and swine, and the valuation is the book's clearest statement of what the law thinks he is. At St Michael's under Thomas Auld he is hungry again, and a Sabbath school for the enslaved is broken up by men who hold church office.

scenes.title: The valuation
scenes.summary: Men, women, children and animals ranked together for division between heirs.

scenes.title: St Michael's
scenes.summary: Thomas Auld's conversion at a camp meeting makes him harder, and the Sabbath school is dispersed with sticks.

structure.label: Chapter X
structure.title: The breaking, and the fight
structure.summary: Hired out to Edward Covey, Douglass is worked and beaten until the reading stops and the wish for freedom goes quiet. In August 1833 he refuses to be whipped, and the two men fight for the better part of two hours. The following year, at William Freeland's, he keeps a Sabbath school of over forty scholars and plans an escape that fails.

scenes.title: Covey
scenes.summary: A man the enslaved called the snake, and six months that reduce Douglass to what he calls a brute.

scenes.title: August 1833
scenes.summary: He repels Covey by force, and is never whipped again in the four years that remain.

scenes.title: The school and the plan
scenes.summary: Forty scholars on Sundays, a forged pass, a betrayal, and Easton jail.

structure.label: Chapter XI
structure.title: North, and paid for the work
structure.summary: Douglass states plainly that he will not describe how he escaped, because the route belongs to people still using it. What he does describe is arrival: the loneliness of New York, the marriage to Anna Murray, the choice of a surname, and the shock of finding New Bedford wealthier than Maryland without owning anybody.

scenes.title: What he refuses to say
scenes.summary: The escape is omitted on principle; the underground railroad, he argues, has been made too public already.

scenes.title: Wages
scenes.summary: Loading a sloop for two silver half-dollars that belong to him, and taking the name Douglass at a breakfast table.

scenes.title: August 1841
scenes.summary: He speaks to a white audience for the first time and is taken up by the anti-slavery societies.

structure.label: Appendix
structure.title: Two religions with one name
structure.summary: Anticipating the charge that he has attacked Christianity, Douglass draws the distinction himself and makes it absolute: the religion of the slaveholder and the religion of Christ cannot both be accepted. The prose turns to parody and catalogue, and the book ends with a signature rather than a scene.

scenes.title: The distinction
scenes.summary: A hymn parody, a list of the slaveholding church's habits, and a closing pledge signed with his chosen name.

characters.name: Frederick Douglass
characters.role: The author, narrator and subject — a real man, writing about his own life
characters.summary: He is at once the child in the story and the practised speaker telling it, and the gap between the two is where the book does its work. He withholds as carefully as he discloses, and the control of tone is itself evidence against the claim that an enslaved man could not have written the book.
characters.clue: He could not tell you his own birthday, learned his letters from a kitchen mistress who was later forbidden to teach him, and took his surname from a poem at a breakfast table in Massachusetts.
traits: deliberate about what he will not say

relationships.label: held by, and instructed by accident

characters.name: Captain Anthony
characters.role: Douglass's first owner, and Colonel Lloyd's clerk and superintendent
characters.summary: A middling man rather than a magnate: he manages another man's plantation and owns a few farms of his own. Douglass never learns his first name, records the rumour that he was his father without settling it, and uses the whipping of Aunt Hester to introduce him.
characters.clue: He kept another man's accounts, owned two or three farms, and is remembered chiefly for what he did in a kitchen at daybreak with a cowskin.

characters.name: Colonel Edward Lloyd
characters.role: Owner of the home plantation on the Wye
characters.summary: He is the scale against which everything in the first four chapters is measured: hundreds of people, a fleet of sloops, a garden that visitors travel to see. Douglass reports that he did not know his own slaves by sight, which the book presents as the natural product of owning that many.
characters.clue: His garden drew sightseers from Annapolis, and he once questioned a man on the road about his master without either of them knowing who the other was.
traits: remote from the people he owns

characters.name: Sophia Auld
characters.summary: She had never owned anyone before, and treated a child as a child, which in this household was the anomaly. Douglass tracks her decline with more care than he gives any other white person in the book: the teaching stops, then the kindness, and finally she is the one snatching a newspaper out of his hands.
characters.clue: She began by teaching a boy the alphabet because it had not occurred to her not to, and ended by watching him to make sure he never read again.

characters.name: Hugh Auld
characters.role: Baltimore shipbuilder, in whose house Douglass lived
characters.summary: He stops the lessons and, in doing so, delivers the clearest analysis of slavery in the book: that literacy and bondage are incompatible. He means it as a household instruction and Douglass receives it as a plan, which is the single most consequential misunderstanding in the Narrative.
characters.clue: He explained to his wife, with a boy in the room, precisely why that boy must never be taught to read — and so told him what to do next.
traits: unguarded in front of a child

relationships.label: holder of, and unintended tutor to

characters.name: Thomas Auld
characters.role: Douglass's legal owner after the division of the estate, at St Michael's
characters.summary: Douglass presents him as a man who was cruel without being good at it, and who became worse after a camp-meeting conversion gave his cruelty religious sanction. It is Thomas Auld who hires Douglass out to Covey for a year, having failed to manage him himself.
characters.clue: He came back from a Methodist camp meeting more pious and more dangerous, and quoted scripture while whipping a lame young woman.

characters.name: Edward Covey
characters.role: A poor farmer who took in men to break them
characters.summary: His trade is reputation: he gets free labour because slaveholders send him people to be subdued, and he keeps the reputation by never letting a fight become public. That is why the two hours in the stable yard finish him — he cannot have Douglass whipped in Easton without advertising his own failure.
characters.clue: The people working his fields called him the snake, because he crawled through the corn to catch them resting.

relationships.label: beaten by, and silenced about it

characters.name: William Freeland
characters.role: Farmer near St Michael's, Douglass's employer in 1835
characters.summary: He is the best enslaver in the book, which the book treats as a problem rather than a relief: he feeds people properly, works them reasonable hours, and makes no religious claims. Douglass plans his escape from this farm, and says so in order to close the argument that kindness answers the objection to slavery.
characters.clue: He fed his workers well, gave them time and tools, and claimed no religion — and it was from his farm that six men planned to steal a canoe and go north.

relationships.label: employer of, and target of the escape plan

characters.name: William Lloyd Garrison
characters.role: Editor of The Liberator, and author of the preface
characters.summary: He heard Douglass speak at Nantucket in 1841 and put him on the anti-slavery lecture circuit. His preface insists the book is wholly Douglass's own work, which was necessary and is also the first sign of a relationship in which a black author keeps being introduced by white men.
characters.clue: He printed the newspaper Douglass subscribed to within months of reaching New Bedford, and later stood up at Nantucket to tell an audience what they had just heard.

themes.name: Literacy as contraband
themes.summary: Reading enters the book as a domestic kindness, is reclassified as a threat within a chapter, and is thereafter pursued as a criminal activity: bread traded for lessons, copybooks worked over at night, a Sabbath school held in a house whose owner cannot be named. Douglass is careful to say it brought no comfort with it.
themes.development: Sophia Auld's lessons in Chapter VI, Hugh Auld's prohibition and its unintended instruction, the torment of Chapter VII, and finally Douglass teaching forty others at Freeland's in Chapter X.

themes.name: Identity and documents
themes.summary: The book begins with an absence of paperwork — no birth record, no acknowledged father, no fixed name — and ends with Douglass choosing a surname over a breakfast table and printing it on a title page. In between, the only document that records him accurately is a valuation listing him with the horses.
themes.development: From the missing record of Chapter I, through the appraisal in Chapter VIII, to the series of names — Bailey, Stanley, Johnson, Douglass — in Chapter XI.

themes.name: Resistance and the body
themes.summary: Douglass makes the decisive event of his life a physical one, and he does not soften it into a metaphor: two hours of fighting in a yard, after which he is never whipped again. He presents it as the recovery of something taken rather than the acquisition of something new, and he dates it.
themes.development: Endurance in Chapters VIII and IX, collapse under Covey in the first half of Chapter X, the fight in August 1833, and the failed escape plan of 1836 planned in cold blood rather than fury.

themes.name: The slaveholding religion
themes.summary: The worst men in the book are the pious ones, and Douglass builds the case in instalments rather than asserting it: Thomas Auld gets crueller after his conversion, class leaders break up a Sabbath school with sticks, and the appendix finally names the pattern. The point is not that religion is false but that it has been captured.
themes.development: The camp meeting in Chapter IX, the destruction of the school at St Michael's, the Sunday piety of Covey in Chapter X, and the systematic distinction drawn in the appendix.

themes.name: Evidence and testimony
themes.summary: Douglass writes as a witness in a proceeding that has no court: he gives names, counties and dates, records three killings that produced no charge, and knows that his evidence will be disbelieved on grounds of who he is. The form of the book is shaped by the standard of proof his readers will apply.
themes.development: The murders of Demby and of Mrs Hicks's girl in Chapter IV, the preface and letter that exist to authenticate him, and the closing pledge in the appendix to rely on the power of truth.

themes.name: Kinship broken by sale
themes.summary: Mothers are hired out twelve miles away, children are separated before they can remember, grandmothers are turned out in the woods when they can no longer work. Douglass argues that these are not incidental cruelties but the mechanism by which an owner secures a claim, and he includes the law that makes a child inherit its mother's condition.
themes.development: The night visits and unmourned death of his mother in Chapter I, the fate of his grandmother in Chapter VIII, and his own refusal in Chapter XI to endanger anyone still held.

techniques.name: Retrospective narration
techniques.definition: A narrator telling their own earlier life, with the distance between the two selves doing the judging.
techniques.inThisBook: Douglass writes as a man on a lecture circuit remembering a child who could not read, and frequently marks the distance: he tells us what he did not then understand, and what he has since learned to call it.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.definition: A narrator or speaker turning outward to address the reader or the audience by name.
techniques.inThisBook: He addresses northern readers who have taken the singing of the enslaved for happiness, and tells them they have made a greater mistake than they know.

techniques.name: Apostrophe
techniques.definition: Speech addressed to something that cannot answer.
techniques.inThisBook: On the banks of the Chesapeake he speaks to the sails on the bay, and the speech is both a rehearsal for the public speaker he will become and the moment he first says out loud that he will run.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: A list allowed to run on past the point of usefulness, so that the accumulation itself becomes the effect.
techniques.inThisBook: The monthly allowance of pork and meal, the annual clothing, the men appraised beside the swine: Douglass repeatedly stops telling a story and lists quantities, because the list is the thing being described.

techniques.name: Scriptural argument
techniques.definition: Using scripture as the ground of an argument rather than as decoration.
techniques.inThisBook: The appendix works by quotation and parody rather than assertion, and Douglass's praise of a New Bedford neighbour is made entirely out of the words of Matthew 25.

techniques.name: Deliberate omission
techniques.definition: Refusing to supply information the reader expects, and saying why.
techniques.inThisBook: The escape itself is not described. Douglass explains the reasoning — a route made public is a route closed — and so converts a gap in the story into a demonstration of what testimony owes to the people still inside it.

quotations.text: Mr. Douglass has very properly chosen to write his own Narrative, in his own style, and according to the best of his ability, rather than to employ someone else. It is, therefore, entirely his own production
quotations.speaker: William Lloyd Garrison
quotations.context: In the preface, before the reader reaches Douglass's first sentence.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a defence, which means it tells you what the accusation was. Garrison has to certify the authorship of a book whose author is standing beside him, and the very act of certifying reproduces the assumption it answers — the reader is being asked to trust a white man about a black man's prose.

quotations.text: I have no accurate knowledge of my age, never having seen any authentic record containing it.
quotations.context: The second sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: An autobiography conventionally opens with a date, and this one opens with the absence of one. The words are the language of evidence — accurate, authentic, record — so the first thing Douglass establishes is not a feeling but a documentary gap, and the rest of the chapter shows that the gap was arranged.

quotations.text: slaveholders have ordained, and by law established, that the children of slave women shall in all cases follow the condition of their mothers
quotations.context: Immediately after reporting the rumour that his owner was his father.
quotations.analysis: He does not pursue the rumour; he cites the statute instead, and the shift from gossip to legislation is the whole method of the book in one move. Naming the law also names the incentive: a rule that makes a man's children his property turns a private crime into an investment.

quotations.text: It was the bloodstained gate, the entrance to the hell of slavery, through which I was about to pass.
quotations.context: On witnessing the whipping of his aunt, as a small child.
quotations.analysis: The image is architectural rather than emotional: a gate is something you go through on the way somewhere, so the beating is presented as an initiation into a place that he had been living in all along without seeing it. The tense does the work — he is about to pass through a door he has already been carried across.

quotations.text: No words, no tears, no prayers, from his gory victim, seemed to move his iron heart from its bloody purpose.
quotations.context: Describing the whipping of his aunt in the kitchen at daybreak.
quotations.analysis: Three refusals in a row, each shorter than a clause needs to be, and then the sentence stops. The triple negative registers a system rather than a temper: appeals of every kind have been tried and none of them is a working part of this arrangement.

quotations.text: This they would sing, as a chorus, to words which to many would seem unmeaning jargon, but which, nevertheless, were full of meaning to themselves.
quotations.context: On the songs sung by people walking to the great house farm.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built as a correction: a first clause in the voice of the overhearing stranger, then a hinge on 'nevertheless', then the truth. Douglass is describing a coded literature that his readers have been in the presence of without noticing, and he is describing his own book at the same time.

quotations.text: Slaves sing most when they are most unhappy. The songs of the slave represent the sorrows of his heart; and he is relieved by them, only as an aching heart is relieved by its tears.
quotations.context: Answering northerners who cite the singing as evidence of contentment.
quotations.analysis: This is the book acting as an expert witness on a disputed piece of evidence, and it wins by explaining the mechanism rather than by protesting. The comparison with weeping is exact: relief is admitted, and the admission is what makes the correction hard to dismiss.

quotations.text: It would forever unfit him to be a slave. He would at once become unmanageable, and of no value to his master.
quotations.speaker: Hugh Auld
quotations.context: Forbidding his wife to continue teaching Douglass to read, with Douglass in the room.
quotations.analysis: The argument against literacy is put in the language of property maintenance — fitness, manageability, value — and it is the most accurate sentence any enslaver speaks in the book. Auld believes he is protecting an asset, and he is in fact reading out the instructions.

quotations.text: From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
quotations.context: Immediately after overhearing Hugh Auld's prohibition.
quotations.analysis: The verb is 'understood', not 'decided': what he has been handed is a map rather than a motive, and he had the motive already. The short declarative closes the scene like a door, and the next seven years of the narrative are spent walking the route it names.

quotations.text: That cheerful eye, under the influence of slavery, soon became red with rage; that voice, made all of sweet accord, changed to one of harsh and horrid discord; and that angelic face gave place to that of a demon.
quotations.context: On the change in Sophia Auld after her husband stops the lessons.
quotations.analysis: Three parallel clauses, each pairing a feature with its ruin, so that a woman is described by the same method Douglass uses for a plantation economy. The agent named in the sentence is not Sophia Auld but slavery, which is the book's consistent claim: ownership damages the owner as reliably as it damages anybody else.

quotations.text: I would at times feel that learning to read had been a curse rather than a blessing. It had given me a view of my wretched condition, without the remedy. It opened my eyes to the horrible pit, but to no ladder upon which to get out.
quotations.context: After reading The Columbian Orator and abolitionist speeches, aged about twelve.
quotations.analysis: The second and third sentences say the same thing twice, once abstractly and once as an image, and the repetition enacts the state it describes: a mind going round something it cannot leave. It also refuses the comfortable version of the story, in which education arrives as deliverance.

quotations.text: The silver trump of freedom had roused my soul to eternal wakefulness.
quotations.context: Describing the period after he could read, when the thought of his condition would not leave him.
quotations.analysis: The trumpet is the one from the resurrection, which makes wakefulness a permanent condition rather than a morning. Read beside the sentences around it — he wishes himself a beast, he envies the stupidity of others — the grandeur of the image is the problem, not the consolation.

quotations.text: Thus ended our little Sabbath school in the pious town of St. Michael’s.
quotations.context: After class leaders broke up a Sunday reading class with sticks and missiles.
quotations.analysis: One flat sentence, and the whole weight rests on the word 'pious', which is doing the work a page of argument would otherwise do. Douglass rarely raises his voice at moments like this; he lets the adjective sit next to the facts and leaves the reader to make the collision.

quotations.text: You are loosed from your moorings, and are free; I am fast in my chains, and am a slave!
quotations.context: Alone on the banks of the Chesapeake, speaking aloud to the sails on the bay.
quotations.analysis: The clause structure is a pair of balanced opposites, and the man speaking it has nobody to hear him but the ships. It is the first speech Douglass ever reports himself making, and it is already built like a platform address — the future lecturer is audible in it years before he has an audience.

quotations.text: I was broken in body, soul, and spirit.
quotations.context: After six months under Edward Covey.
quotations.analysis: Three nouns, no qualification, and the passive voice admitting that it worked. Douglass gives the defeat its own paragraph before he gives the fight one, and the ordering matters: the recovery in August only counts because he has let the reader see the man who had stopped wanting to read.

quotations.text: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
quotations.context: Introducing the fight with Covey, halfway through the longest chapter in the book.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a chiasmus, and it turns on its axis exactly where the book does. Note that both halves are passive: a man is made, and then made again, so even the recovery is described as something done to him — the agency arrives in the next paragraph, with his hands.

quotations.text: This battle with Mr. Covey was the turning-point in my career as a slave. It rekindled the few expiring embers of freedom, and revived within me a sense of my own manhood.
quotations.context: Immediately after the two-hour fight in the stable yard.
quotations.analysis: 'Career' is a startling word to apply to being owned, and it is chosen: it insists that the years had a shape and that he can analyse them. Both verbs — rekindled, revived — describe the return of something that existed before Covey, which is how Douglass avoids making freedom a thing granted to him by an event.

quotations.text: It was a glorious resurrection, from the tomb of slavery, to the heaven of freedom.
quotations.context: Describing what the fight with Covey did to him.
quotations.analysis: He takes the central image of the religion his enslavers profess and applies it to an act of physical violence against one of them. That is the argument of the appendix made in a single phrase, four chapters early, and it is why the book cannot be read as a quarrel with Christianity.

quotations.text: In coming to a fixed determination to run away, we did more than Patrick Henry, when he resolved upon liberty or death. With us it was a doubtful liberty at most, and almost certain death if we failed.
quotations.context: On the six men who planned to take a canoe up the Chesapeake in 1836.
quotations.analysis: He does not ask to be compared to a founding patriot; he asserts that the comparison undersells him, and then supplies the arithmetic. Addressed to American readers who kept Patrick Henry's sentence on their walls, the claim converts a national slogan into a test its owners have failed.

quotations.text: They came because they wished to learn. Their minds had been starved by their cruel masters. They had been shut up in mental darkness.
quotations.context: On the Sabbath school he kept at William Freeland's, which grew to over forty scholars.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is deliberately physical — starved, shut up — and it matches the accounting of pork and meal earlier in the book, so that a withheld education is placed in the same ledger as a withheld ration. Every one of those scholars risked thirty-nine lashes to attend, which Douglass mentions without adjective.

quotations.text: I have never approved of the very public manner in which some of our western friends have conducted what they call the underground railroad
quotations.context: Opening the final chapter, explaining why he will not describe his escape.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is tactical, not moral: he goes on to honour the courage of the people he is criticising. What the sentence establishes is that the author has a professional judgement about what may be printed, which quietly rebuts the idea that a witness owes the reader everything he knows.

quotations.text: I felt like one who had escaped a den of hungry lions.
quotations.context: Quoting a letter he wrote to a friend on reaching New York in September 1838.
quotations.analysis: He quotes his own younger self rather than describing the feeling directly, and then immediately undercuts it: the elation subsides within a paragraph into insecurity and loneliness among thousands of strangers. The structure refuses the ending that the escape narrative is expected to supply.

quotations.text: I must hold on to that, to preserve a sense of my identity.
quotations.context: Letting Nathan Johnson choose him a surname in New Bedford, on condition that the first name stays.
quotations.analysis: He has been Bailey, Stanley and Johnson within a fortnight, and the surname that reaches the title page is picked out of Walter Scott by a man he has just met. Against all that, the retained forename is the whole of the continuity he has, and he says so in the vocabulary of ownership: hold on, preserve.

quotations.text: I love the pure, peaceable, and impartial Christianity of Christ: I therefore hate the corrupt, slaveholding, women-whipping, cradle-plundering, partial and hypocritical Christianity of this land.
quotations.context: Opening the appendix, written to forestall the charge that he is an enemy of religion.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built as a balance with a hinge — 'I therefore hate' — so that the hatred is presented as a consequence of the love rather than an alternative to it. The second half runs to six adjectives against the first half's three, and the compounds are all crimes, so the prose is weighted the way the argument is.

timeline.label: Frederick Bailey born in Talbot County, Maryland
timeline.detail: The date is now generally given as February 1818, though the book opens by saying he has never seen a record of it.

timeline.label: Sent from the Eastern Shore to Baltimore
timeline.detail: He was about eight. The move put him in Hugh and Sophia Auld's house, where the lessons began.

timeline.label: The fight with Edward Covey
timeline.detail: Dated in the book to one of the hottest days of August, after six months of being hired out to a man paid in labour to break people.

timeline.label: Escape to New York, and marriage to Anna Murray
timeline.detail: The book gives the marriage certificate in full and says nothing whatever about the journey.

timeline.label: First speech to a white audience, at Nantucket
timeline.detail: On 11 August, at an anti-slavery convention; Garrison's preface begins from that meeting.

timeline.label: The Narrative published in Boston
timeline.detail: Issued by the Anti-Slavery Office with Garrison's preface and Wendell Phillips's letter attached.

timeline.label: British supporters purchase his legal freedom
timeline.detail: Raised during a lecture tour of Britain and Ireland undertaken partly because the book had made him traceable.

timeline.label: Douglass founds The North Star in Rochester
timeline.detail: His own paper, and the beginning of his separation from Garrison's wing of the movement.

timeline.label: My Bondage and My Freedom
timeline.detail: A longer second autobiography, written without a white sponsor's preface and less willing to be a specimen.

timeline.label: The Emancipation Proclamation
timeline.detail: Douglass recruited for the Union army and pressed Lincoln on the pay and treatment of black soldiers.

timeline.label: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass
timeline.detail: The third autobiography, which finally describes how the escape was made.

timeline.label: Douglass dies in Washington
timeline.detail: On 20 February, after a lifetime of public office, journalism and speaking.

places.name: Easton, Talbot County, Maryland
places.note: The county town twelve miles from Tuckahoe, where Douglass was born, and where he was later held in jail after the failed escape.

places.name: Baltimore
places.note: The Aulds' house, the alphabet, the shipyards, and the city he escaped from in 1838.

places.name: St Michaels, Maryland
places.note: Thomas Auld's town, where the Sabbath school was broken up by class leaders.

places.name: Chesapeake Bay
places.note: The water whose sails Douglass addressed from the bank, and the route north he planned by canoe.

places.name: New Bedford, Massachusetts
places.note: The whaling port where he was first paid for his own labour and took the name Douglass.

places.name: Nantucket
places.note: The 1841 anti-slavery convention at which he spoke for the first time to a white audience.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest way of reading it, and the one the book invites: a deposition offered to a hostile jury, full of names, counties and dates precisely because the witness expects to be disbelieved.
criticalViews.counter: Read only as testimony, its craft disappears — and the craft was the point, since the prose itself was the exhibit the doubters had to explain away.

criticalViews.summary: Criticism from the 1970s onwards has treated the Auld scene as the centre of the book and the whole narrative as an account of how a person acquires the means to describe his own situation.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the story too neatly redemptive, when Douglass says flatly that reading tormented him and gave him no way out for years.

criticalViews.summary: Later readers have paid close attention to the fact that two white men speak for thirty pages before Douglass speaks at all, and have read his later autobiographies as an escape from that arrangement as much as from Maryland.
criticalViews.counter: The sponsorship was also the reason the book reached a mass readership and stayed in print, and Douglass used the platform before outgrowing it.

criticalViews.summary: The fight with Covey is described as the recovery of manhood, and the women in the book — his mother, his grandmother, his aunt, Anna Murray — are largely suffering or offstage.
criticalViews.counter: The pattern may belong to the genre and its audience rather than to Douglass's opinion, and later black women's narratives were written partly in answer to it.

essayQuestions.question: How does Douglass turn a personal history into an argument about a national system?
plan: Start from the opening: an absence of records presented as data rather than as complaint.
Show the movement from scene to analysis in Chapters III and IV, where three killings are followed by the observation that no charge followed any of them.
Use the catalogues — the food allowance, the clothing, the valuation in Chapter VIII — to show economics doing work that indignation cannot.
Examine the direct addresses to northern readers on the songs and the singing, where the reader is told they have misread evidence they already had.
Close on the appendix, which generalises from named individuals to a national religious culture.

essayQuestions.question: 'Literacy in the Narrative is a wound as much as a weapon.' Discuss.
plan: Set out the Auld scene in Chapter VI and the exactness of the prohibition's reasoning.
Trace what reading actually delivers in Chapter VII: abolitionist vocabulary, and unbearable clarity about a condition he cannot leave.
Weigh the phrase 'a curse rather than a blessing' against 'the pathway from slavery to freedom', both in the same fifteen pages.
Bring in the Sabbath schools at St Michael's and Freeland's, where literacy becomes collective and therefore punishable.
Conclude with the book itself as the final act of literacy, and with what it cost Douglass to publish it under his own name.

essayQuestions.question: Why does Douglass refuse to describe his escape, and what does the refusal achieve?
essayQuestions.focus: Withholding, danger and the ethics of testimony
plan: Open with Wendell Phillips's letter, which frames publication itself as physical risk.
Set out Douglass's stated reason: a route made public is a route closed to the next person.
Consider the effect on the reader, who is denied the climax the genre promises and given a principle instead.
Compare the naming of enslavers, which is generous with danger to himself, against the silence about helpers.
Weigh the 1881 Life and Times, where the escape is finally described, and ask what had changed.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of the appendix?
essayQuestions.focus: Religion, hypocrisy and the shape of the book
plan: Note first that it is a defence against an objection Douglass expects, and answers it before it is made.
Gather the evidence already laid: Thomas Auld after the camp meeting, the class leaders at St Michael's, Covey's Sunday piety.
Analyse the rhetoric of the opening sentence, where love and hatred are placed on either side of one hinge.
Consider the hymn parody and what it assumes about the reader's familiarity with the original.
Decide whether the appendix completes the argument or protects it, and whether the book would be weaker without it.

discussionQuestions: Douglass opens by listing what he does not know. Why begin an autobiography with an absence?
Hugh Auld's prohibition is the most accurate account of slavery given by any white person in the book. What does it mean that the analysis comes from that direction?
The fight with Covey changes nothing legally. Why does Douglass make it the turning point?
Two white abolitionists speak for thirty pages before the author does. How should a modern reader take the preface and the letter?
William Freeland is the kindest owner in the book, and Douglass plans his escape from Freeland's farm. What is being argued there?

related.why: Published seven years later and read by the same public: an abolitionist novel set against a first-person account by a man who had been enslaved.
The same Mississippi valley world from the other side, with a boy learning to disobey the law Douglass was written against.
Another American book of the 1840s and 50s about public judgement, religious authority and who is permitted to speak.
Twain on the legal fictions of race and inheritance, half a century after Douglass set out the law that made a child follow its mother.
A later argument about who is allowed the conditions to write, and what the absence of a record does to a life.
